specPoints.text: understand reasons for the trend in reactivity of the elements down Group 1 (Li to K) and Group 2 (Mg to Ba)
know the reactions of the elements of Group 1 (Li to K) and Group 2 (Mg to Ba) with oxygen, chlorine and water

primer.text: Reactivity in Groups 1 and 2 climbs as you descend: outer electrons sit further out, feel weaker attraction, and leave sooner. This note follows both groups into oxygen, chlorine and water, tabulates the alkali metal products, and sets out the Group 2 equations including the steam reaction that turns magnesium vigorous.

lessons.title: Why the descent quickens the reaction
lessons.opening: Both groups grow more reactive as atoms get bigger. This lesson traces the mechanism: each new shell pushes the outer electron out, the attraction weakens, less energy pops the electron off, and the reaction quickens.
keyPoints: Group 1 reactivity increases down the group as each atom only needs to lose one electron.
Losing the outer electron leaves a full shell beneath, giving the ion noble gas configuration.
Down the group the outermost electron sits further from the nucleus with weaker attraction.
Less energy is needed to remove the electron as the attraction weakens.
Group 2 reactivity climbs for the same reason, magnesium reacting extremely slowly with cold water.

low.restatement: More shells mean the outer electron orbits further out and feels less pull, so it leaves more easily and the metal reacts more vigorously down the group.
low.analogy: A kite on a longer string flies further from your hand and takes less tug to redirect - each new shell lengthens the string.
low.examPointer: Write the causal chain in order: further away, weaker attraction, less energy, lost more easily - the sequence carries the marks.

medium.restatement: Shell addition increases both the radius and the shielding between nucleus and outer electron, so the ionisation enthalpy falls; the activation barrier for the first step of every reaction drops with it, quickening both groups identically.
medium.analogy: A vending machine with the snack closer to the flap dispenses faster - the electron's distance to the exit shrinks in energy terms each period.
medium.examPointer: For the water comparison, quote the observed contrast: magnesium extremely slow in cold water, calcium fairly vigorous and exothermic.

check.stem: What configuration does a Group 1 ion reach after losing its outer electron?

options.text: Noble gas configuration, because the shell beneath is already full
options.explanation: The exposed inner shell completes the stable arrangement.
The remaining shells are full, not half.

options.text: A configuration with one electron still exposed
options.explanation: The single outer electron is the one lost.
Ionisation changes the electron count.

check.stem: Why does the outer electron's attraction weaken down the group?

options.text: It sits further from the nucleus behind more shells
options.explanation: Distance plus shielding both grow.
Proton count rises down the group.
Electron properties are fixed.
Each added shell expands the atom.

check.stem: Which observation contrasts magnesium and calcium in cold water?

options.text: Magnesium reacts extremely slowly while calcium reacts fairly vigorously
options.explanation: The observed pair marks the trend.
Neither is explosive in cold water.
Calcium clearly reacts.
The order is the reverse.

check.stem: Why does calcium's water reaction being exothermic fit the trend?

options.text: Easier electron loss releases the metal's stored reactivity more readily, warming the mixture
options.explanation: Faster reaction releases heat faster.
The example is vigorous.

options.text: Heat proves calcium is less reactive
options.explanation: Vigour marks the higher reactivity.

options.text: Cold water cannot give exothermic reactions
options.explanation: It can, as calcium shows.

check.stem: Which phrase completes: as you descend Group 1, the outer electron is lost...

options.text: more easily, because the attractive force it feels is weaker
options.explanation: Weaker pull, easier exit.

options.text: less easily, because the attractive force is stronger
options.explanation: Both halves are inverted.

options.text: at the same rate all the way down
options.explanation: The rate clearly climbs.
No catalyst is involved.

check.stem: State the reactivity trend of Group 1 down the group.
check.modelAnswer: The reactivity of Group 1 metals increases down the group.

check.stem: Quote the calcium water-reaction description.
check.modelAnswer: Calcium's reaction with cold water is fairly vigorous and exothermic.

check.stem: Explain why the same argument covers both groups.
check.modelAnswer: Both groups react by donating outer electrons, so whatever lowers the cost of that donation - growing radius and shielding - raises reactivity identically in both families.

check.stem: If each added shell roughly halves the attraction the outer electron feels, estimate the attraction at the third element down relative to the first.
check.modelAnswer: Two halvings leave one quarter of the original attraction, which is why the third element reacts so much more readily.

lessons.title: Alkali metals meet oxygen and water
sourceHeadings: Summary of the Reactions of the First Three Alkali Metals with Oxygen
Summary of the Reactions of the First Three Alkali Metals with Water
lessons.opening: The alkali metals tarnish in air and fizz in water, faster the further down you look. This lesson tabulates the first three metals' products with oxygen and water, and adds the chlorine reaction that mirrors oxygen in appearance.
keyPoints: Alkali metals tarnish in air because oxygen converts their surface to a dull oxide coating.
Tarnishing speeds up as you descend the group.
With chlorine, Group 1 metals burn with the same flame colours as in oxygen, forming white chlorides: 2M + Cl2 -> 2MCl.
With water the vigour climbs down the group, producing hydroxides and hydrogen.
The summary tables list each metal's oxide product and its water-reaction vigour.

low.restatement: Fresh cuts dull over in seconds because oxygen coats them; in water they skitter and fizz, and both behaviours intensify down the group.
low.analogy: Cut apples browning in air: the exposed surface meets oxygen and changes - the alkali metals just do it far faster, and faster still the lower they sit.
low.examPointer: Name the products precisely: metal oxide with oxygen, metal hydroxide plus hydrogen with water, metal chloride with chlorine.

medium.restatement: The oxide layer forms by the same electron donation as every other reaction, so the falling ionisation cost shows up as faster tarnishing and more violent water reactions; the chloride equation 2M + Cl2 -> 2MCl conserves the 1:1 metal-to-chloride ratio.
medium.analogy: Three runners on a wet track, the lower group members wearing better grip shoes: same race, same rules, quicker finish down the ladder.
medium.examPointer: Balance the chlorine equation by inspection: two metals surrender two electrons to one Cl2, so 2MCl needs the coefficient 2.

check.stem: Why do alkali metals tarnish in air?

options.text: Oxygen converts the exposed surface into a dull oxide coating
options.explanation: The coating is the tarnish.
The oxide, not dissolution, is the change.
The primary tarnish is oxide.
Metals do not evaporate on the bench.

check.stem: What happens to the rate of tarnishing down the group?

options.explanation: Faster oxidation tracks the reactivity climb.
The trend quickens downward.
The reactivity trend rules it out.
No reversal exists.

check.stem: What equation describes a Group 1 metal reacting with chlorine?

options.explanation: Two metals fill one chlorine molecule's two slots.
Group 1 ions are +1, so MCl2 is wrong.
Chlorine travels as Cl2 molecules.
Free Cl atoms are not the reactant.

check.stem: What forms when an alkali metal reacts with water?

options.text: The metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas
options.explanation: The fizz is the hydrogen escaping.
Water supplies hydrogen, not oxygen gas.
Chloride needs chlorine, absent here.
The vigorous fizzing shows otherwise.

check.stem: How do the flame appearances compare for Group 1 metals burning in oxygen versus chlorine?

options.text: They are similar, as sodium's intense orange flame shows in both gases
options.explanation: The appearance carries over between the two oxidants.

options.text: Oxygen gives no flame but chlorine does
options.explanation: Both produce the metal's characteristic flame.
The metal burns in it.

options.text: Only the lightest metals burn at all
options.explanation: The whole group reacts.

check.stem: State what coats an alkali metal surface exposed to air.
check.modelAnswer: A dull coating of the metal oxide covers the surface, which is the tarnish.

check.stem: Write the general equation for a Group 1 metal with chlorine.
check.modelAnswer: 2M (s) + Cl2 (g) -> 2MCl (s), a white solid in each case.

check.stem: Explain why tarnishing accelerates down the group.
check.modelAnswer: Tarnishing is oxidation by air, so the same falling ionisation cost that quicken the water reactions also speeds oxygen capture at the surface.

check.stem: Sodium burns in chlorine with an intense orange flame. If 2.3 g of sodium (1 mole of atoms per 23 g) reacts fully, how many moles of Cl2 does it consume?
check.modelAnswer: The equation 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl pairs 2 Na atoms with 1 Cl2, so 1 mole of sodium atoms consumes 0.5 moles of chlorine molecules.

lessons.title: Group 2 equations: water, oxygen, steam
sourceHeadings: Group 2 Metals Reacting with Water and Oxygen - Equations
lessons.opening: Group 2 writes its own equation set: oxides with oxygen, hydroxides with water, and the steam exception that makes magnesium vigorous. This lesson walks the table, including the peroxide footnote for strontium and barium.
keyPoints: The general oxygen equation is 2M + O2 -> 2MO for any Group 2 metal.
Strontium and barium also form peroxides, MO2, alongside the oxides.
The general cold-water equation is M + 2H2O -> M(OH)2 + H2, except beryllium which never reacts.
Magnesium reacts extremely slowly with cold water but vigorously when heated in steam.
With chlorine, Group 2 metals form the metal chloride, as in Mg + Cl2 -> MgCl2.

low.restatement: Group 2 metals burn to oxides, fizz to hydroxides and hydrogen in water, and pair with chlorine one-to-one; magnesium needs steam to show its vigour, and the two heaviest members add a peroxide option.
low.analogy: A family of swimmers: everyone crosses the pool (reacts) at their own pace, the lightest needs heated water to swim at all, and the two heaviest sometimes wear double armbands (peroxides).
low.examPointer: Quote the steam equation separately - Mg + H2O(g) -> MgO + H2 - and mark the state change from liquid to gaseous water.

medium.restatement: The oxide route conserves the 2:1 metal-to-oxygen-molecule ratio; the water route doubles water per metal to supply two hydroxide ions; peroxides arise when the heavier cations stabilise the O2 2- unit instead of the oxide lattice.
medium.analogy: Same currency, two denominations: the oxide route pays in single O2- coins, the peroxide route in one doubled O2 2- coin, and only the richest cations (Sr, Ba) can float the bigger note.
medium.examPointer: In peroxide items, name the ion explicitly - MO2 means the peroxide O2 2-, not two separate oxide ions.

check.stem: What is the general equation for a Group 2 metal reacting with oxygen?

options.explanation: Two metals join one oxygen molecule.
That is the peroxide route, not the general one.
Oxygen travels as O2 molecules.
Group 2 oxides are MO, not M2O.

check.stem: Which Group 2 metals additionally form peroxides with oxygen?

options.explanation: SrO2 and BaO2 appear beside the oxides.
The lightest pair stick to oxides.
Beryllium barely reacts at all.
The peroxide option opens only for the heavy pair.

check.stem: Why does beryllium not appear in the cold-water equation?

options.text: It does not react with water
options.explanation: Be sits out the water reaction entirely.

options.text: It reacts too violently to write safely
options.explanation: The opposite: it never reacts.
No such species exists.

options.text: It floats away from the water
options.explanation: Density is not the reason.

check.stem: What changes for magnesium between cold water and steam?

options.text: It reacts extremely slowly cold but vigorously in steam, forming MgO and H2
options.explanation: Heating the water to steam unlocks the vigour.

options.text: It reacts vigorously cold but not in steam
options.explanation: The order is reversed.
Steam gives the oxide, not a peroxide.
Steam clearly accelerates it.

check.stem: What does magnesium form with chlorine gas?

options.explanation: Mg + Cl2 -> MgCl2 conserves the charges.
Magnesium ions are +2, needing two chlorides.
No hypochlorite forms in direct combination.
Oxygen plays no part.

check.stem: Write the general cold-water equation for Group 2 metals.
check.modelAnswer: M (s) + 2H2O (l) -> M(OH)2 (s or aq) + H2 (g), except for beryllium.

check.stem: State the peroxide footnote of the oxygen reactions.
check.modelAnswer: Strontium and barium also form the peroxides SrO2 and BaO2 alongside their oxides.

check.stem: Explain why steam enables magnesium's vigorous reaction while cold water does not.
check.modelAnswer: Steam carries far more thermal energy and contacts the metal as a gas, so the surface oxide barrier breaks and the MgO + H2 reaction runs vigorously where cold water's slow attack never gets started.

check.stem: Calcium reacts per Ca + 2H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + H2. How many moles of hydrogen form from 2 moles of calcium?
check.modelAnswer: The 1:1 metal-to-hydrogen ratio gives 2 moles of H2 from 2 moles of calcium.

glossary.definition: The dull oxide coating that forms on an alkali metal surface exposed to air.
The MO2 species, holding the O2 2- ion, formed by strontium and barium alongside their oxides.
Magnesium's vigorous reaction with gaseous water, forming magnesium oxide and hydrogen.
